name: Assumed similarity bias
statement: People judging a stranger's personality import their own self-description into the judgement, and the effect persists after the coded behaviour of both people is controlled.
meaning: The measure is a correlation, not an estimate about a population. A perceiver describes their own personality, describes a target, and the two descriptions are compared across items or traits. In the Social Relations Model the same idea is fitted across a group: Kenny defines assumed similarity as the correlation between a person's self-perception and their perceiver effect, which is how they rate everyone on average. The claim is that the first description leaks into the second. Hughes and colleagues treat it as separable from actual similarity, citing Human and Biesanz, who controlled for actual similarity and still found the association. It is also separable from the false consensus effect, entry 10, which asks for the percentage of a population sharing a two-way choice and then compares that percentage between people who chose differently.

origin.note: Cronbach did not coin the phrase. His own reference list gives Fiedler's 1954 paper on assumed similarity measures as the example of the formula, and he notes Fiedler's ASo variant, computed between two others rather than between self and other. Fiedler's own report confirms it, defining ASo as assumed similarity between opposites, taken across a judge's predictions for his liked and disliked choices. What Cronbach added was the algebra that took the score apart. The version read for this entry is the August 1954 technical report, no. 10 of the Group Effectiveness Research Laboratory at the University of Illinois, written under an Office of Naval Research contract with Fiedler as principal investigator. Its title drops the words 'scores on' that the published article carries.

evidence: Cronbach defines the squared assumed similarity score as the sum, over items, of squared differences between a judge's rating of another person and that judge's rating of himself. He splits it into four terms: assumed elevation, assumed dispersion in elevation, assumed self-typicality, and assumed dispersion within items. Assumed elevation asks whether the judge places others at his own average level on the scale. Assumed self-typicality asks whether the judge treats his own profile shape as typical. The two dispersion terms measure how far the judge expects others to differ from one another, and Cronbach recommends pairing each with its neighbour. The same components sit inside accuracy scores, so a correlation between measured empathy and measured projection follows from the arithmetic. Cronbach's verdict on one published set of such correlations is that they would arise even where both sets of responses are determined strictly by chance, and that they have no psychological meaning. His illustrative decomposition uses eight judges and eight others. Hughes, Flournoy and Srivastava tested the modern version in 2021. 322 previously unacquainted people self-reported on the Big Five Inventory 2, met a stranger at least a day later for a 20-minute art gallery task, and afterwards rated that stranger. Their model estimates the direct path from a perceiver's own trait to their perception of the partner, holding the coded behaviour of both people constant. That path was positive in all five domains and in 9 of 15 facets. Agreeableness was the largest, an unstandardised 0.197 with a 95% interval of 0.116 to 0.285, standardised at .25. The other four ran from .16 for neuroticism down to .10 for extraversion.

examples.tag: The stranger rated from your own answers
examples.text: A man who describes himself as anxious and orderly fills in the same questionnaire about someone he met for ten minutes, and the two sets of answers line up more closely than ten minutes could account for.

examples.tag: The quiet colleague who must dislike crowds
examples.text: Someone who avoids large gatherings assumes a quiet new colleague avoids them too. He may well be right, which is the awkward part of the name: where the other person really is alike, a self-anchored guess is a good guess.

examples.tag: The panel that agrees with itself
examples.text: Interviewers who describe themselves as direct tend to describe candidates as direct. What is shared across all of one interviewer's ratings is a feature of the rater, which is why the effect shows up in an average rather than in one judgement.

replication.headline: A preregistered dyadic study of 322 strangers found assumed similarity in all five Big Five domains, largest for agreeableness at a standardised path of .25, with both people's coded behaviour held constant.
replication.detail: Hughes, Flournoy and Srivastava separate three routes to perceived similarity, and the traditional one survives. Alongside it runs what they call state assumed similarity: the perceiver's own behaviour during the task predicted how they saw the partner, with the partner's behaviour held constant. It was .11 for agreeableness and .10 for energy level. The paper's text gives .17 for neuroticism on that path, while its own table prints .01 for the same cell, so that figure is left unsettled here. The authors stress that this route is not interpersonal, because it rests on the perceiver's own conduct. The interpersonal route is a double-mediated path, in which a perceiver expresses a trait, draws matching behaviour out of the partner, and then reads that behaviour accurately. It was supported for sociability, for openness and for the organisation facet of conscientiousness, at .02 each, and ran the other way for assertiveness at -.02. For agreeableness it was 0.001, 95% interval -0.002 to 0.005. Part of what looks assumed is therefore elicited, and the authors call every compound effect small. Kenny and West's meta-analysis of 24 studies is the standing summary of the correlational literature. Only its abstract was read here, at PubMed; Sage answers the article with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall notice. Kenny's own summary page puts the correlation of self-perception with the perception of one other at .25, against .27 for the similarity a perceiver sees between two others, and states the second is statistically the larger. Those two figures are quoted from that page rather than from the paper, and they are not in the fields above.

study.cite: Hughes, B. T., Flournoy, J. C., & Srivastava, S. (2021). Is perceived similarity more than assumed similarity? An interpersonal path to seeing similarity between self and others. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 121(1), 184-200.

limits: Cronbach's illustrative analysis rests on eight judges, and he writes that correlations based on eight cases cannot be interpreted confidently. His paper is algebra: he says so, describing the method as almost entirely algebraic analysis based on a model rather than on actual behaviour. The Hughes study is one laboratory, one 20-minute task and one sample of previously unacquainted people. Its preregistration covered agreeableness, openness and the extraversion facets; the neuroticism and conscientiousness models were planned as exploratory, and the other facet models were not preregistered at all. The authors call the compound effects small, then argue that a small effect can still matter if the process repeats outside the laboratory. Their 'suggestive rather than a basis for strong conclusions' wording belongs to the state assumed similarity paths, not to the compound ones. The Kenny and West figures were not read off the paper. A larger problem sits under any raw similarity score, and Wood and Furr set it out. Most of an overall profile similarity is the normative profile, the description that fits almost anybody. In their roommate sample the average overall similarity was .68, and the average distinctive similarity, after subtracting the normative profile from both sides, was .10. The two rankings of the same people correlated .42. Overall similarity, personality stability and judgement agreement all correlated with one another at .26 or above; the distinctive versions correlated at .08 or below in absolute value. Overall roommate similarity correlated .28 with satisfaction with life, and distinctive similarity -.01. Their correlations rest on between 93 and 151 people, and the copy read here is the author manuscript at PubMed Central rather than the published version. Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC and OSF on 21 September 2026 found no multi-laboratory replication of the Social Relations Model estimate of assumed similarity.
misreadings: The name promises an error and the measure does not deliver one. Where the target really does resemble the perceiver, a self-anchored judgement is a correct judgement. Hughes and colleagues make the sharper version of the point: in a live interaction a perceiver can produce the similarity they then perceive, so some of the correlation is elicited rather than assumed. It is not the false consensus effect, entry 10, although the two are filed together and Kenny lists false consensus among the names assumed similarity travels under. False consensus compares the population estimates of two groups who chose differently on a two-way item, and needs no target. Assumed similarity correlates one person's self-description with their description of a particular other person, and needs no second group. Nor is it psychological projection, entry 43, whose Freudian sense requires the perceiver to be denying the trait, nor social projection, entry 548, which is about groups. The last error is to read the raw number as a quantity of bias. Wood and Furr's roommate figures, .68 overall against .10 distinctive, are the size of the gap between the two readings.

sources.text: Cronbach, L. J. (1955). Processes affecting scores on "understanding of others" and "assumed similarity." Psychological Bulletin, 52(3), 177-193. Read in full, but as the August 1954 University of Illinois technical report no. 10, titled without the words 'scores on' and scanned at the Internet Archive. The published article was not obtained, and the two versions were not compared.

Fiedler, F. E. (1954). Assumed similarity measures as predictors of team effectiveness. The Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 49(3), 381-388. Cited by Cronbach as the example of the assumed similarity formula. Read as Illinois technical report no. 6, titled 'Assumed similarity measures as predictors of team effectiveness in surveying', in a declassified Defense Documentation Center scan. The published article was not obtained, and the two versions were not compared.

Cronbach, L. J., & Gleser, G. C. (1953). Assessing similarity between profiles. Psychological Bulletin, 50(6), 456-473. The profile-distance paper Cronbach's decomposition builds on, and reference 10 of his 1954 report. Read as the 1952 Illinois report 'Similarity between persons and related problems of profile analysis', which sets out the elevation, scatter and shape decomposition. The published article was not obtained.

Hughes, B. T., Flournoy, J. C., & Srivastava, S. (2021). Is perceived similarity more than assumed similarity? An interpersonal path to seeing similarity between self and others. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 121(1), 184-200. Accepted manuscript read in full at PsyArXiv, dated to its acceptance in August 2020; source for every path coefficient quoted here. The version of record at APA answered with a refusal, so the two were not compared.

Kenny, D. A., & West, T. V. (2010). Similarity and agreement in self- and other perception: A meta-analysis. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 14(2), 196-213. Abstract read at PubMed. The publisher's page answers with a Cloudflare bot challenge, not a paywall notice. On 21 September 2026 no open copy was found at Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Europe PMC, OpenAIRE, CORE, the Wayback Machine, ResearchGate or the authors' own pages.

Kenny, D. A. (2021). Interpersonal Perception: Assumed Similarity. Author's summary page for chapter 7 of Interpersonal Perception: The Foundation of Social Relationships. The only source read here for the .25 and .27 figures from the 2010 meta-analysis.

Wood, D., & Furr, R. M. (2016). The correlates of similarity estimates are often misleadingly positive: The nature and scope of the problem, and some solutions. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 20(2), 79-99. Full text read, as the NIH author manuscript at PubMed Central rather than the version of record; source for the normative-desirability confound and the roommate figures.
